# Randomized controlled clinical study evaluating the efficacy and safety of intratumoral treatment of canine mast cell tumors with tigilanol tiglate (EBC-46)

Thomas R De Ridder^{  1 }, Justine E Campbell^{  1 }, Cheryl Burke-Schwarz^{  2 }, David Clegg^{  3 }, Emily L Elliot^{  4 }, Samuel Geller^{  5 }, Wendy Kozak^{  6 }, Stephen T Pittenger^{  7 }, Jennifer B Pruitt^{  8 }, Jocelyn Riehl^{  2 }, Julie White^{  9 }, Melissa L Wiest^{  10 }, Chad M Johannes^{  11 }, John Morton^{  12 }, Pamela D Jones^{  1 }, Peter F Schmidt^{  1 }, Victoria Gordon^{  1 }, Paul Reddell^{  1 }
## Abstract

Objective: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of tigilanol tiglate (TT) for local intratumoral treatment of mast cell tumors (MCTs) in dogs.

Methods: A randomized controlled clinical study in 2 phases involving 123 dogs with cytologically diagnosed MCT. Phase 1 compared 81 TT-treated dogs with 42 control dogs; phase 2 allowed TT treatment of control dogs and retreatment of dogs that failed to achieve tumor resolution after TT treatment in phase 1. Tigilanol tiglate (1 mg/mL) was injected intratumorally with dose based on tumor volume. Concomitant medications were used to minimize potential for MCT degranulation. Modified response evaluation criteria in solid tumors were used to evaluate treatment response at 28 and 84 days. Adverse events and quality of life were also assessed.

Results: A single TT treatment resulted in 75% complete response (CR) (95% confidence interval [CI] = 61-86) by 28 days, with no recurrence in 93% (95% CI = 82-97) of dogs by 84 days. Eight TT-treated dogs that did not achieve CR in phase 1 achieved CR after retreatment, increasing the overall CR to 88% (95% CI = 77-93). Control dogs had 5% CR (95% CI = 1-17) at 28 days. Wound formation after tumor slough and wound size relative to tumor volume were strongly associated with efficacy. Adverse events typically were low grade, transient, and directly associated with TT's mode of action.

Conclusions: Tigilanol tiglate is efficacious and well tolerated, providing a new option for the local treatment of MCTs in dogs.

## Study title

Engaging the Immune System to Kill Solid Tumors in Pet Dogs - A Comparative Oncology Approach (TriKE + Radiation Therapy)

## Purpose of study

The purpose of the study is to identify a safe and effective dose of a novel immunotherapy drug (TriKE) when given with hypofractionated radiation therapy (RT) in companion dogs with a sarcoma. 

## Eligibility criteria

Dogs must: 

  * Have cytologically or histopathologicaly confirmed sarcoma, measuring at least 2cm
  * Weigh at least 7 kg (15 lbs)
  * Modified performance score less than 2 and expected survival of at least 2 months
  * Have no metastasis (local/regional lymph node involvement may be included at discretioin of PI)
  * Have no significant co-morbidities that affect heart, lung, kidney, or liver function
  * Not be currently receiving chemotherapy or radiation treatment (previous ok with a washout period)
  * Not have previous immunotherapy (previous cytopoint is allowed) 

## Procedures

Screening visit:  physical exam, tumor measurements, chest x-rays and CT scan of chest and abdomen for staging under general anesthesia, blood and urine collection, flow cytometry using blood and tumor samples

Radiation therapy (RT) treatment days 0-4:  physical exam, tumor measurements, RT given under general anesthesia; day 4 blood for labs collected, flow cytometry using blood and tumor samples

Immunotherapy treatment days 18, 21, 24, 28, 31, 35:  physical exam, tumor measurements, TriKE given under the skin and observed up to 2 hours after; day 18, 35 blood and urine collection, flow cytometry using blood and tumor samples, chest x-ray on day 35

Rechecks around days 11, 42, 60-90, 150-180, 240-270, 330-360:  physical exam, tumor measurements, blood collection for labs and flow cytometry; some visits will include re-staging with chest x-rays and CT scan of chest/abdomen under general anesthesia

## Costs

The dog’s owner is responsible for costs associated with diagnosis to allow enrollment. 

Once enrolled, the study will cover all costs associated with participation, including blood and urine tests, flow cytometry, CT scans, chest x-rays, radiation planning CT, radiation therapy treatments, immunotherapy treatments, and follow-up exams. The cost of initial staging, including blood and urine tests, imaging (chest x-rays and CT scan) will be covered by the study if performed at the Veterinary Medical Center.

## Explore Current Research Trials in Canine Oncology

When a beloved dog is diagnosed with cancer, many families ask whether a clinical trial may provide an additional option. Canine oncology studies are conducted throughout the United States and around the world, but identifying an appropriate trial, and participating in one, can sometimes be challenging.

Each clinical trial has specific eligibility requirements.

These may include: 

  * A dog’s breed
  * Age
  * Weight
  * Overall health
  * Life expectancy
  * Cancer type
  * Cancer stage
  * Previous care
  * ...and other medical factors

Meeting a study’s general description does not guarantee acceptance. Pet parents should speak directly with the research team and their veterinary care provider to determine whether a trial may be appropriate for their dog.

It is also important to understand that clinical trials are not always free.

Research funding may cover only certain tests, medications, procedures, or appointments.

# Canine T-cell Lymphoma Trial

## Biodynamic Testing of Chemotherapy Sensitivity in Dogs Receiving Gemcitabine for Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma

### Principal Investigator

Dr. Michael Childress, Professor of Comparative Oncology

### Background

Epitheliotropic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (ETCL) in dogs is a skin cancer for which few effective therapies exist. The chemotherapy drug gemcitabine is commonly used to treat humans with this cancer. Although gemcitabine has been shown to be well-tolerated in dogs, its use as a treatment for dogs with ETCL has not been described.

In this clinical trial, we will enroll 10 dogs with ETCL to test the efficacy of gemcitabine against this cancer. In addition, we will test the ability of a novel tissue imaging technology, biodynamic imaging (BDI), to predict the responsiveness of ETCL to gemcitabine.

We have shown in previous studies BDI predicts the response of primary nodal lymphomas in dogs to chemotherapy with approximately 80-90% accuracy. This will be the first time that BDI is used to predict the response of canine ETCL to a chemotherapy drug.

# COOL - Clinical Trials

At the Comparative Oral Oncology Laboratory (COOL), our research bridges discovery and clinical patient care. Through targeted clinical trials, we offer novel diagnostic and therapeutic strategies for companion animals facing oral cancers.

## Active Trial: Novel Targeted Oral Therapy for Canine Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma (OSCC)

Squamous Cell Carcinoma is the second most common oral malignancy in dogs. Because these tumors are locally invasive, rapidly erode bone, and frequently recur following conventional treatments, surgical options are sometimes limited.

This study evaluates Trametinib, an FDA-approved targeted oral medication used in human oncology. Having established its safety in dogs, our goal in this expanded trial is to identify specific molecular and genetic profiles that predict favorable treatment response, allowing us to deliver precise, effective targeted therapy.

## Modiano Lab clinical trials

Modiano lab clinical trials are facilitated by the College of Veterinary Medicine's Clinical Investigation Center (CIC). The CIC is the central location for veterinary clinical trials and translational research studies for faculty at the College. Learn more about the CIC on their website

### Other clinical trials

Visit the University of Minnesota’s Clinical Investigation Center, for current enrollment information for all pet animal clinical trials.

### About clinical trials

Clinical trials, or clinical studies, take place in the clinic, a step after lab research studies. They offer experimental treatments to patients who fit the criteria of a particular study and are used to determine whether new drugs or treatments are both safe and effective.

There is some risk with any clinical trial, just as with many medical procedures; however, all clinical trials are reviewed by an Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) before they can begin. Also, informed owner consent is always part of clinical trials, so before your pet enters a study you will be given all information up front and must agree in writing. In many clinical trials, patients must be treated at the clinic conducting the trial and may not receive study drugs remotely.

Research ethics at the University of Minnesota. We are committed to protecting research participants, upholding ethical standards, and improving our practice at every step of our work.

# SBRT for Canine Lung Tumor Study

< BACK TO ALL CLINICAL-TRIALS

  * Recruiting
  * Dog
  * Oncology

Primary pulmonary carcinomas in dogs are most commonly treated with surgery, which can result in survival times of approximately one year. Stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) is a highly precise form of radiation therapy that delivers high doses of radiation directly to a tumor while minimizing exposure to surrounding normal tissues. The purpose of this study is to evaluate dogs with primary pulmonary carcinoma treated using a standardized SBRT protocol across institutions participating in the Veterinary Radiation Therapy Oncology Group (VRTOG).

## Inclusion Criteria

Dogs are eligible for enrollment if they meet all of the following criteria:

  * Cytologic or histopathologic diagnosis of a single primary pulmonary carcinoma.
  * Primary lung tumor measuring greater than 1 cm in its shortest diameter.
  * No previous treatment for the lung tumor.
  * No diagnosis of another malignant tumor outside the lungs within 30 days before enrollment.

# Clinical Trial Development

## Synopsis of the NCI Comparative Oncology Trial Consortium

Image: two people with a pet dog

The Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium (COTC) is an active network of nineteen academic comparative oncology centers, centrally managed by the NIH-NCI-Center for Cancer Research's Comparative Oncology Program, that functions to design and execute clinical trials in dogs with cancer to assess novel therapies. The goal of this effort is to answer biological questions geared to inform the development path of these agents for future use in human cancer patients. Trials conducted by the COTC are pharmacokinetically and pharmacodynamically rich with the product of this work directly integrated into the design of current human Phase I and II clinical trials. Our trials are carried at COTC member institutions, which currently include 19 sites. See examples of published COTC trials.
